eligibility.exact_action_basis: H.R.29 would extend the federal mandatory-custody category to the following offenses: burglary, theft, larceny or shoplifting. The four listed property-offense terms take the meaning assigned by the jurisdiction where the acts occurred. The exact bill adds an INA 236(c) mandatory-custody category requiring inadmissibility under INA 212(a)(6)(A), (6)(C), or (7) together with a specified criminal predicate: being charged, arrested, convicted, admitting commission, or admitting acts constituting the essential elements. These inadmissibility categories concern presence without admission/parole or undesignated arrival, material immigration fraud/false citizenship claims, and specified entry-document defects, subject to their existing statutory qualifications. DHS must issue a detainer for a person meeting the new ground and, if the person is not otherwise detained by Federal, State or local officials, effectively and expeditiously take custody. The bill also gives a State attorney general or other authorized State officer standing, on alleged harm to the State or residents (including financial harm in excess of $100), to seek appropriate injunctive relief in district court over five specified federal matters: INA 235(b)(1)/(2) detention/removal requirements; INA 236 release, bond or parole decisions; the existing INA 243(d) visa-discontinuance requirement for countries denying or unreasonably delaying acceptance; violation of the existing INA 212(d)(5)(A) case-by-case urgent-humanitarian/significant-public-benefit parole limits; and INA 241(a)(2) detention during the removal period. Courts must advance and expedite these cases to the greatest practicable extent. INA 236(e) removes its express release/grant shield while leaving the other printed discretionary-judgment/detention/revocation/denial restrictions, and INA 242(f)(1) receives an exception for the printed listed actions, while its separate final-removal-order injunction standard remains. These review changes do not establish a general right to enjoin every immigration action. The parole clause changes its named administering actor to the Secretary of Homeland Security. The baseline removal period is generally 90 days with specified starting/extension conditions; the bill adds litigation standing over its detention requirement rather than creating that period. The pre-existing narrow protection-release exception remains, redesignated as INA 236(c)(4), including its witness/potential-witness/cooperator and immediate-family/close-associate categories, no-danger/appearance conditions and offense-severity procedure.

The exact House-passed H.R.23 requires the President, not later than 60 days after enactment and on an ongoing basis, to impose sanctions if the ICC is attempting to investigate, arrest, detain or prosecute a protected person. Covered foreign persons are those the President determines directly engage in or aid such an effort; materially assist, sponsor or provide specified support/goods/services for it; or are owned/controlled by, or currently act or purport to have acted for, a person directly engaging in it. For covered aliens, the bill makes them inadmissible, ineligible for visas or other entry documents, admission or parole, and any other INA benefit. Their visas/entry documents must be revoked regardless of issuance date, effective immediately and automatically canceling other valid visas/entry documents in their possession. The immigration sanctions also apply to each sanctioned foreign person's spouse, parent, sibling or adult child; the separate property-blocking requirement applies to the principal foreign persons described in 3(a)(1). Foreign person means someone other than the defined United States person, which includes U.S. citizens, lawful permanent residents, U.S.-organized entities and any person in the United States. The incorporated INA alien definition excludes U.S. citizens and nationals. Protected persons include any defined U.S. person unless the United States both formally consents to ICC jurisdiction and is a Rome Statute party. They also include foreign citizens or lawful residents of a NATO or designated major non-NATO ally that has not consented to ICC jurisdiction or is not a Rome Statute party. The listed military/government personnel are inclusive examples, not the entire protected class. The President may waive sanctions case by case for periods no longer than 90 days each on a reported vital-national-security determination before the waiver takes effect, including the specified detailed rationale and actions by the United States and ICC. The President may terminate sanctions on written certification that the ICC has ceased all covered efforts and permanently closed/withdrawn/ended/terminated them. Imposition also requires congressional briefing/written notice within 10 days. The package includes property blocking under existing IEEPA authorities and penalties, rescission of available ICC appropriations at enactment and a prospective ban on using appropriated funds for the ICC. Immigration membership follows the direct travel/admission/parole/benefit restrictions, not the foreign-affairs findings. These are proposed legislative requirements; existing general INA inadmissibility/temporary-admission authorities are not treated as newly created by this bill. Actual designation, visa revocation, sanctions, enforcement or enactment is not inferred.

The exact House-passed H.R.30 adds INA 212(a)(2)(J) inadmissibility for a person convicted of, admitting commission of, or admitting acts constituting the essential elements of a sex offense under 34 USC 20911(5), or a conspiracy to commit one. New 212(a)(2)(K) uses those same conviction/admission predicates for a crime of domestic violence (defined through 237(a)(2)(E)), stalking, child abuse/neglect/abandonment, or a crime violating the protective-order portion addressing credible threats, repeated harassment or bodily injury. The INA baseline makes these inadmissibility grounds relevant to visas and admission; the bill is not limited by its title to persons unlawfully present. It separately adds INA 237(a)(2)(G) deportability for conviction of a defined sex offense or conspiracy: admission of conduct alone is not the predicate in this new deportability clause. The existing 237(a)(2)(E)(i) after-admission conviction ground for domestic violence, stalking and child abuse/neglect/abandonment remains; its domestic-violence definition is expanded to include any crime constituting domestic violence under 34 USC 12291(a), regardless of whether the jurisdiction receives grants. Noncriminal behavior mentioned in the victim-services portion of that definition is not itself converted into a crime by this bill. The incorporated sex-offense definition covers criminal sexual-act/contact offenses, specified offenses against minors, listed federal/military offenses, and attempts/conspiracies, with its foreign-conviction fairness and consensual-conduct limitations. The latter exclude specified consensual adult conduct unless custodial authority exists, and specified conduct where the victim is at least 13 and the offender is not more than 4 years older. Some covered conduct already can trigger existing criminal inadmissibility or deportability grounds; these are additional grounds and a definition expansion, not the creation of all immigration consequences for these crimes. INA 101(a)(48) supplies the existing conviction framework, including specified withheld adjudications with a guilt/plea/facts predicate plus court-ordered punishment, penalty or restraint. H.R.30 references 20911(5), rather than expressly importing the separate 20911(8) juvenile-conviction definition. The bill leaves the 237(a)(7) discretionary battered-person waiver for specified domestic-violence/stalking/protective-order deportability grounds intact; that waiver is not written to cover the new sex-offense ground. Existing 212(d)(3) discretionary temporary nonimmigrant admission and 212(d)(13)/(14) T/U status waiver authorities remain within their own conditions. Existing 212(h) enumerates other criminal grounds and is not expanded to the newJ/K grounds. No universal waiver or automatic removal is established. The new 237(a)(2) deportability ground sits within the existing 237(a) framework for an alien (including a crewman) in and admitted to the United States, with removal upon the specified government order. It is not a universal new deportability ground for every unadmitted alien. INA 101 distinguishes immigration admission (lawful entry after inspection/authorization) from admitting criminal conduct; parole alone is not admission. This governing status scope is separate from any offense's after-admission timing element. No individual admission status or actual removal order is inferred.

The exact House-passed H.R.35 adds 18 USC 40B: operating a motor vehicle within 100 miles of the United States border while intentionally fleeing a pursuing U.S. Border Patrol agent acting under lawful authority, or a pursuing Federal/State/local officer actively assisting or under Border Patrol command. The ordinary penalty alternatives are imprisonment up to 2 years, a title 18 fine, or both; where serious bodily injury results the imprisonment alternative is 5–20 years, and where any person's death results it is 10 years to life, with fine-or-both alternatives retained in both cases. The bill adds INA 212(a)(2)(J) inadmissibility and 237(a)(2)(G) deportability for any alien convicted of, admitting commission of, or admitting acts constituting the essential elements of 40B(a). It also inserts 208A making a person meeting that same predicate ineligible for relief under the immigration laws, expressly including asylum under 208. Neither arrest alone nor merely being within 100 miles is the printed immigration predicate. Pre-existing 18 USC 758 already criminalizes vehicle flight/evasion from an immigration or other federal checkpoint followed by fleeing law-enforcement agents above the legal speed limit, with up-to 5 years/fine/both; existing 237(a)(2)(A)(iv) already makes a conviction for 758 deportable. H.R.35 creates a different officer/geography/intent predicate and additional immigration consequences, rather than the first-ever immigration checkpoint-flight offense or deportability ground. Unlike that existing deportability ground, the newG also accepts specified admissions. Existing INA 101(a)(48) conviction rules remain. The Attorney General, with the Secretary of Homeland Security, must report annually to both Judiciary Committees on violations, charged/apprehended/not-charged/not-apprehended counts, and penalties sought/imposed. A reporting duty is not evidence of actual violations, convictions or enforcement. The separate broad relief-bar clause is preserved as printed; it is not replaced by a blanket claim that existing narrow waivers guarantee relief, and no individual asylum or removal outcome is decided. The new 237(a)(2) deportability ground sits within the existing 237(a) framework for an alien (including a crewman) in and admitted to the United States, with removal upon the specified government order. The exact H.R.495 EH proposal adds “and annually thereafter” to Public Law 117-263 section 7134(a)(2), after “development of the strategic plan”. The Commissioner of U.S. Customs and Border Protection would therefore report on implementation of the existing counter illicit cross-border tunnel operations strategic plan not later than one year after its development and annually thereafter, to the House Homeland Security and Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committees. The pre-existing 7134(a)(1) already requires the Commissioner, coordinating with the DHS Science and Technology Under Secretary and appropriate DHS officials, to develop the plan within 180 days of the 2022law. Its existing scope includes risk-based identification/breach/assessment/remediation criteria, technologies and community impacts, information sharing, Border Patrol sector indicators and technology/staffing needs. H.R.495 changes the reporting cadence, not those plan requirements. The separate 6 USC 257 annual report on discovered Mexico–U.S. tunnels and DHS prevention/investigation/prosecution needs already exists and is not the provision amended here. Existing 7134(b) authorized$1 million for each of fiscal 2023 and 2024 for plan development and remediation; H.R.495 neither extends that authorization nor supplies new appropriations. Membership follows direct border-tunnel operations reporting. Actual reporting, tunnel remediation, border outcomes or enactment are not established by the House suspension-and-passage vote.

The exact H.R.993 EH proposal requires the DHS Secretary, acting through the CBP Commissioner and DHS Science and Technology Under Secretary, to submit a plan within 180 days of enactment to the House Homeland Security and Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committees. The plan is to identify, integrate and deploy emerging/advanced technologies to enhance or address gaps in border-security operations. Its prescribed contents cover innovation-team use and composition, contributions and coordination, technologies from other agencies, procurement authorities and need for alternatives, scaling programs, program goals/timelines, border-community privacy/security impacts, replacement costs, research/private-sector coordination, metrics and listed aircraft/surveillance/inspection/tunnel/communications technologies. The bill gives the CBP Commissioner express authority to maintain one or more innovation teams to research and adapt new/emerging commercial technologies for border capability gaps and urgent mission needs, and assess potential outcomes including negative consequences where documented gaps are yet to be determined. It requires each maintained team to establish operating procedures, defined roles/partner relationships and transition protocols, plus strategic planning with costs, timeframes, metrics and performance parameters, including technology-transition rates. The Commissioner must report within 180 days and annually thereafter to the same committees on team procedures/plans, technologies piloted in the preceding fiscal year, success/gap determinations and status of transitioning successful technologies. This provides statutory authority and prescribed planning/reporting for maintaining teams; it does not establish that innovation teams or pilots first come into existence with this proposal. The technology list and planned deployment goals are not universal mandates to deploy every technology. No appropriation, universal pilot success or actual operational outcome is stated. Membership follows the express direct border-operations scope rather than DHS administration alone.

The exact H.R.22 EH proposal adds documentary proof of United States citizenship to covered NVRA federal voter-registration applications, including motor-vehicle, mail and designated-agency routes. The proposed definition accepts: a REAL ID-consistent identification that indicates U.S. citizenship; a valid U.S. passport; military ID together with a service record showing U.S. birth; valid Federal/State/Tribal photo ID showing U.S. birth; or other valid such photo ID together with specified certified birth, contemporaneous hospital-birth, adoption, consular-birth, naturalization/citizenship/other INA-issued proof, or DHS American Indian Card with KIC classification. The birth-certificate route has seven printed content/issuance/file/signature/seal requirements. Not every REAL ID, military ID, Tribal ID or American Indian card alone qualifies. Mail applicants must present proof in person by the State application deadline, or at a permitted same-day/early-voting polling place no later than election day, with notice/instructions and reasonable disability accommodations. Each State subject to the new provisions must establish an alternative process for an applicant without the listed documentary proof: signed citizenship/eligibility attestation under perjury plus other evidence and a State/local official determination, accompanied by the official's affidavit using EAC minimum standards/basis. A separate discrepancy-documentation process is required. The bill does not eliminate these alternatives or itself decide a particular document/name/status case. Covered States must take ongoing citizenship-check steps and establish the specified verification program within 30 days. State-requested necessary citizenship-verification information, including requested batches, must be supplied by a Federal agency head possessing it within 24 hours without a fee; Federal agencies share information to respond, and the specified sources include existing DHS SAVE, SSA verification, State-ID and other confirmation databases. The bill also directs DHS to investigate whether to initiate INA 239 removal proceedings if an INA-defined alien is determined through the specified information routes to be unlawfully federally registered. This is an investigation-to-determine duty, not automatic commencement or an actual removal order. States must remove confirmed noncitizens from federal voter rolls on documentation/verified information, with the proposed citizenship-ground exception to the existing 90-day systematic-roll-removal deadline; removing a voter record is not deportation. Existing INA unlawful-voting grounds concern actual unlawful voting with their own conditions and parent/residence/reasonable-belief exceptions; they do not turn registration alone into universal removability. INA 237 also retains its admitted-person framework. The INA alien definition excludes U.S. citizens and nationals; a noncitizen U.S. national is not automatically an alien. Section 5 additionally requires prompt DHS naturalization notice to the chief election official where the individual is domiciled. NVRA attestation/citizenship eligibility and the qualified 18 USC 611 alien-voting prohibition already exist; the proposal adds proof/verification and related duties rather than first banning every noncitizen vote. General passport issuance includes persons owing U.S. allegiance whether citizens or not; the bill's valid-passport proof route is preserved as printed without asserting that every passport holder is a citizen or creating citizenship. Existing SAVE is a benefit/status-verification system with privacy protections and a statutory prohibition on administrative noncriminal immigration-enforcement use. H.R.22 references that existing system and adds the investigation duty but does not expressly repeal the prohibition; their legal interaction and individual data-use/enforcement outcomes are preserved for review rather than silently resolved as a blanket repeal. The bill adds an express missing-proof-registration violation to NVRA civil notice/enforcement remedies and inserts material assistance by an executive employee to a noncitizen, or missing-proof registration, into the existing criminal provision. Its knowingly-and-willfully depriving/defrauding-election-process chapeau and maximum 5-year/fine-or-both framework are retained, not strict liability for every paperwork error. Existing private notice/cure rules remain 90 days,20 days for violations within 120 days of a federal election, and no prior notice for violations within 30 days. It adds limited criminal/immigration-proceeding exceptions to registration-office confidentiality, with the printed knowledge wording differing between motor-vehicle and Federal-mail clauses. EAC guidance is due within 10 days; voter-material changes are exempted from the Paperwork Reduction Act. Proposed applicability preserves the no-registration State exemption and printed special same-day-registration-State provisions, which refer to NVRA 8(i)/(j), not silently substituted 8(j)/(k). The bill's SAVE-use subparagraph refers to requests under paragraph(1), while the express request provision appears in(5)(A); this printed cross-reference is disclosed rather than silently repaired. Provisional-ballot ability/counting is preserved for individuals verified as citizens under new 8(j), and exemptions from non-NVRA Federal law are unaffected. The proposal takes effect on enactment and applies to applications submitted on/after that date. The whole House passage choice covers this complete scheme and its election/immigration interactions; no individual citizenship determination, registration denial, voter purge, offense, removal, effect on participation or enactment is inferred.

The complete H.R.36 EH is a Georgia foreign-policy, reporting, assistance and sanctions package. Its operative section6 adds two conditional immigration-sanctions routes, independently of the nonbinding findings/policy language. Under6(b), within 90 days of enactment the President must determine whether the specified foreign persons knowingly engaged in significant corruption or violence/intimidation in relation to blocking Georgia Euro-Atlantic integration. The covered groups are people who served in Parliament on/after January 1, 2014 or current/former senior Georgian-party officials; people currently serving in Government leadership, including law-enforcement, intelligence, judicial and local/municipal leadership; and the defined immediate family members who benefitted from the specified officials/persons conduct. An affirmative decision requires6(d)(2) sanctions; it is not a designation of every Georgian official or relative. The Secretary of State must brief within 90 days with persons and specific supporting facts. A6(b) case waiver requires the President to determine and report national-security interests or sufficiently changed circumstances; the bill states no 180-day maximum for that route. Under6(c), presidential determinations on/after enactment cover responsibility, complicity, direct/indirect engagement or attempts in actions/policies intended to undermine Georgia peace, security, stability, sovereignty or territorial integrity; leaders/officials of entities whose organization or members engaged in those activities; and the defined benefitting immediate family members of sanctioned persons. This route permits property blocking and requires the immigration sanction, plus briefing/written notice within 10 days of imposition. Its separate waiver is renewable for no more than 180 days per period, with national-security determination and written justification submitted at least 15 days before effectiveness. Section6(d)(2) makes a qualifying foreign person THAT IS AN INA ALIEN inadmissible, ineligible for visa/entry documentation, admission, parole and any other INA benefit; revocation of visa/entry documents regardless of issuance date takes immediate effect and cancels other valid entry documents. Foreign person excludes the bill-defined U.S. person: citizens, lawful permanent residents, U.S.-organized entities including foreign branches, and ANY person within the United States. INA alien excludes citizens and U.S. nationals; admission and parole remain distinct. Knowingly includes actual knowledge or should-have-known. The bill defines immediate family by EXPRESS INA201(b)(2)(A)(i) but prints the different8 USC1201 citation. The named INA provision is8 USC1151 and defines immediate relatives of U.S. CITIZENS (children, spouses, parents with citizen aged 21 or older), with qualified surviving-spouse/child and abuse-self-petition retention. This is not the simple spouse/parent/sibling/adult-child list in H.R.23. The citizenship framework and foreign-person exclusion create an application question preserved for review; the candidate does not silently repair the citation or select individuals. The bill also preserves authorized/reportable U.S. intelligence exceptions; an international-obligation exception where admission OR parole is necessary; and qualified agricultural/food/medicine/device/humanitarian transactions and related activity, including the printed6(i)(2)(C)(ii) reference to paragraph(1), not an invented universal actor exemption. No importation-of-goods sanctions authority is added. Existing IEEPA powers, exceptions and other designation authority are not made novel by the package. Section6(g) requires a broader determination and180-day report for POTENTIAL existing-IEEPA sanctions, not a second mandatory visa designation for all corruption. Necessary rules are due within 120 days with 10-day advance congressional notice. Section6(h) terminates a person sanction at certification of ceased conduct or the printed sunset reference to section7; section7 actually concerns conditional additional assistance/contacts/cooperation, with should-language, whereas section8 states the ACT ceases effect five years after enactment. Both literal provisions and the mismatched reference are retained for review, not treated as a new perpetual power or an accepted correction. Reports/assistance and other package purposes remain part of this suspension-and-passage vote. No actual corrupt conduct, sanctioned status, denial, removal, spending outcome or enactment is inferred.

The complete H.R.1503 EH combines international policy, human-rights reporting, passport authority and a mandatory sanctions-list scheme. Section4 permits, rather than requires, the Secretary of State to refuse a passport or revoke a previously issued passport only for an individual convicted under42 USC274e, still subject to imprisonment, parole or other supervised release from that conviction, who used a passport OR crossed an international border in committing that offense. Existing274e concerns knowing acquisition/receipt/transfer of a human organ for valuable consideration for human transplantation affecting interstate commerce, with the qualified paired-donation exception and exclusions for reasonable medical/handling expenses and donor travel/housing/lost wages. That predicate is not synonymous with every coercive harvesting allegation; conviction, continuing sentence/supervision and travel/document nexus are conjunctive. Its existing criminal punishment is not newly enacted here. Existing22 USC211a gives State passport-issuance authority under prescribed rules and country-use restrictions with exceptions, while212 permits passports to persons owing U.S. allegiance, including eligible nationals. The new express qualified authority is not a finding that State previously lacked every denial/revocation power. Section5 adds forced-organ-harvesting/organ-trafficking assessments to existing2151n(d) and2304(b) human-rights reports, not a wholly new reporting institution: existing State reporting has its own country scope, February 25 annual duty in2151n(d), and fiscal-year security-assistance presentation in2304(b). The bill prints an assessment in EACH foreign country, and its definitions/treatment of two subsection (i) labels are preserved rather than narrowed by inherited report headings. Section6 requires the President within 180 days of enactment to send the named congressional committees a list of each person presidentially determined to fund, sponsor or otherwise facilitate the defined forced harvesting or trafficking. That list predicate does not require the passport provision conviction. Person includes individuals, entities and the cited non-state actors: nonsovereign entities with significant political power/territorial control outside sovereign-government control, often using violence. Forced harvesting means organ removal through coercion, abduction, deception, fraud or abuse of power/vulnerability. Trafficking means recruitment, transport, transfer, harboring or receipt for organ removal by those means or controller payments/benefits. Organ incorporates274e(c)(1), including the listed human/fetal organ categories and Secretary-added organs. Listed persons face mandatory property blocking under IEEPA, without1701 emergency-declaration prerequisites. Section6(b)(2) is HEADED aliens, but its operative body says IN THE CASE OF AN INDIVIDUAL: inadmissibility, no visa/entry documentation, no admission/parole/other INA benefit, and immediate revocation regardless of issuance date cancelling other valid documents. The bill supplies no foreign-person exclusion or blanket U.S.-person principal exemption. Its separate U.S.-person definition (citizen/LPR/U.S. entity including foreign branch) describes property possession/control, not who can be listed. The candidate preserves heading/body and INA-alien/national framework without claiming citizens lose citizenship/entry rights or deciding individual applicability. No family sanction is stated. Necessary admission to comply with the UN headquarters, Vienna consular or other treaty/international agreement is excepted. Humanitarian sale/assistance/finance/transport transactions are excepted with their printed scope; no universal humanitarian immunity for every person or unrelated activity is inferred. No importation-of-goods sanctions authority is added. The President may waive sanctions/restrictions case by case for periods at most 180 days each, certifying VITAL national-security interests at least 15 days before effectiveness. Existing IEEPA implementation/penalty framework remains source-qualified, with criminal willfulness and conviction distinct from listing and civil enforcement. This whole-bill suspension-and-passage episode does not establish a component preference, actual forced harvesting, criminal conviction, designation, passport loss, immigration removal or enactment.

This May22 House passage is the whole H.R.1 reconciliation package, not a separate immigration-only vote. The controlling House choice uses H.Res.436: Rules Committee Print119-3 modified by the amendment printed in H.Rept.119-113 was considered adopted. The retained Immigration clauses are reconstructed against that chain and the contemporaneous as-amended floor Record. The currently served EH incorporates later corrections and renumbering and is a comparison witness for these unchanged selected clauses, not the controlling entire vote-time text. Later engrossment corrections and the July Senate replacement are not silently substituted for this choice. The description selects border infrastructure, detention, State reimbursement and asylum-fee mechanisms; it does not inventory every immigration-related tax, benefit, employment-authorization, child-sponsor or removal provision in this multi-domain package. Section60001 would make additional fiscal2025 CBP appropriations available until September30,2029: $46.5billion for primary/waterborne/secondary barriers, access roads and associated detection attributes; a separate $50million for specified invasive plants impeding RioGrande border operations; and $5billion for CBP facilities/checkpoints near the southwest, northern and maritime borders. These are different purposes, not one immigration-enforcement account or actual expenditures. The adopted manager amendment adds section60004: $12billion in additional fiscal2025 DHS funds, available until September30,2029, for grants reimbursing States for costs of actions on or after January21,2021 assisting federal border/immigration enforcement, including detention/removal and combating unlawful entry of persons/contraband. Applications need satisfactory cost evidence, and DHS cannot reimburse a State already reimbursed under another DHS grant program. This is funding subject to a process and conditions, not proof of State awards or a newly conferred State removal power. Section70101 would appropriate an additional $45billion for fiscal2025 to ICE, available until September30,2029, solely for single-adult alien detention and family residential-center capacity. DHS MAY detain family units pending a removal decision and, if ordered removed, until removal. Its family-center definition includes accompanied alien children, excludes unaccompanied alien children, and expressly applies regardless of State/local facility licensing. Its single-adult detention standards clause says they shall be set in the Secretary's SOLE discretion. Preserve that printed language without importing the Senate's express consistent-with-applicable-law qualification or deciding its interaction with judicial/other legal constraints. The existing unaccompanied-child definition in6USC279(g)(2) requires no lawful immigration status, age under18, and no US parent/legal guardian or none available for care/physical custody; childhood alone does not establish that category. Capacity funding and permission are not a universal detention mandate, removal order or actual detention outcome. Section70002 would require an additional fee at the time an alien files an asylum application: the fiscal2025 amount may be set by rule but cannot be less than $1,000. It cannot be waived/reduced. From fiscal2026 its amount increases using the prior fiscal-year fee and the printed July-to-July CPI-U increase, with the increment rounded down to a multiple of $10. Half of the Attorney-General-filed receipts go to EOIR; half of DHS-filed receipts go to USCIS's existing Immigration Examinations Fee Account; those credited amounts may be retained/spent without further appropriation, and the remainder goes to Treasury. Section70010 separately requires a fee for EACH CALENDAR YEAR an application remains pending, initially at least $100 for fiscal2025, with later CPI-U adjustment, Treasury disposition and no waiver/reduction. Its printed adjustment has no express rounding term; the filing-fee rounding rule is not copied into it. These are separate filing and pending-application charges, not fixed lifetime amounts or a claim that every asylum applicant actually paid. Section70023 changes existing INA208(d)(3)/8USC1158(d)(3) from MAY impose fees to SHALL, strikes the following cost-cap/installment/nonmandatory-fee language and preserves authority to set additional adjudication/naturalization fees under286(m). The existing paragraph already allowed fees for asylum consideration, employment authorization and asylum-based adjustment and capped them at adjudication costs; the bill does not create first-ever fee authority or establish a new substantive asylum eligibility test through that edit. Existing1356(m)/(n) supply the account/cost-recovery context. Employment-authorization provisions are separate from asylum filing and annual pending-application fees. House70003 would charge an additional fee on initial employment-authorization applications for asylum applicants underINA208(d)(2), paroled aliens and applicants underTPS244(a)(1)(B). Each initial fee has a fiscal2025 floor of$550, may be higher by DHS rule, cannot be waived/reduced and has the printed fiscal2026-onward July-to-July CPI-U increment rounded down to$10. All three initial authorizations would last no more than six months. In70003(a)(4), the House allocation sentence says25percent of fees received UNDER THIS SECTION goes to USCIS's existing fee account to retain/spend without further appropriation, with50percent of that credited amount for benefit-fraud detection/prevention; uncredited amounts go to Treasury. The separately printed parole/TPS subsections direct their fees to Treasury. Preserve those exact scope words rather than silently deciding their interaction. House70012 and70014 separately impose additional parole/TPS employment-authorization renewal or extension fees with fiscal2025$550floors, possible higher rule amounts, subsequent CPI increments rounded down to$10, Treasury disposition and no waiver/reduction. Both initial and renewed/extended authorizations in those sections last no more than six months. House70013 imposes at least$550 for each asylum-based renewal/extension, Treasury disposition and no waiver/reduction; that section prints no annual inflation formula. DHS MAY provide asylum-applicant employment authorization for at most six months, and each renewal/extension also has that limit. Authorization terminates immediately after an asylum-officer denial unless referred to an immigration judge;30days after an immigration-judge denial unless timely appealed to BIA; or immediately after BIA denies an appeal of asylum denial. House70007 imposes a separate additional sponsor-placement fee, collected by HHS from the individual BEFORE placing an unaccompanied alien child underTVPRA235(c). House70020 imposes ANOTHER additional sponsor fee BEFORE the unaccompanied child's release to the sponsor. House70021 requires a separate fiscal2025 fee of at least$5,000, possibly higher by rule, on an alien BOTH ordered removed in absentia under1229a(b)(5) AND subsequently arrested by ICE. It has later CPI increments rounded down to$10, Treasury disposition and no waiver/reduction, and does not apply if the underlying order was rescinded under1229a(b)(5)(C). House70022 separately charges any INADMISSIBLE alien at the time CBP apprehends the person BETWEEN PORTS OF ENTRY; its fiscal2025 floor is$5,000 or higher by rule, later CPI increments rounded down to$10, Treasury disposition and no waiver/reduction. The complete pre-vote1229a(b)(5) and(e) retain the written-notice rule and failure-to-provide-address exception, clear/unequivocal/convincing evidence of notice and removability, and separate rescission routes: a motion within180days showing exceptional circumstances beyond the alien's control, or at any time for missing statutory notice or no-fault failure while in federal/state custody. House70004 adds a parole-entry fee with fiscal2025floor$1,000 or a higher DHS rule amount, fiscal2026-onward July-to-July CPI-U increments rounded down to$10, Treasury disposition and no waiver/reduction for an applicable fee. It applies to each alien paroled into the US EXCEPT where the alien establishes one of the printed parole-reason exceptions; fee exceptions are not erased by the separate waiver bar. The law-enforcement significant-public-benefit exception requires a DHS determination that significant public benefit has resulted or will result from the parole, BOTH assistance to the USGovernment AND presence required in that matter, PLUS at least one of inadmissibility, failure to meet nonimmigrant-admission eligibility, or insufficient normal-visa time; it is not every asserted public benefit. House exception9 separately requires a Cuban national LIVING IN CUBA, an approvedINA203(a) petition, no immediately available immigrant visa, all immigrant-visa eligibility requirements, no other inadmissibility AND a parole grant furthering the printed US minimum-annual-legal-migration commitment under the1994/1995Cuba-USagreements. House 70009 separately adds a fee on ANY alien applying for Form I-94, with fiscal 2025 minimum $24 or a higher DHS rule amount, later July-to-July CPI-U increments, no expressly printed increment-rounding rule, and no waiver/reduction. House 70017 amends the existing ESTA fee, rather than creating the travel-authorization System or treating it as admission. The exact H.R.2931 EH proposal requires the SBA Administrator to relocate each covered office in a defined sanctuary jurisdiction, but only after making and publishing that office-location determination before ordering relocation. The destination must not be in such a jurisdiction. The jurisdiction definition is a political subdivision of a State with an effective statute, ordinance, policy or practice restricting a government entity/official from exchanging or maintaining specified citizenship or lawful/unlawful immigration-status information with Federal/State/local entities, or complying with a lawfully made DHS detainer or release-notice request under INA 236 or 287. Independent Immigration membership follows these express status-information and lawful-request cooperation conditions, not the SBA label or alleged community crime. The relocation deadline is 120 days after the public determination, not after enactment. If the office has not moved by that deadline, its head must provide a written explanation within 5 days; operations cease from the next day until relocation, and employees are assigned to another covered office in the same State outside a defined sanctuary jurisdiction if one exists, otherwise to another such office. The Administrator must immediately remove the office head if the explanation is absent or the reasons are determined insufficient. The Administrator also cannot establish a covered office in a defined sanctuary jurisdiction. Covered office includes regional/district/local offices other than headquarters, or other fully congressionally funded SBA components under the printed definition. Existing 15 USC 633(a) already allows branch/regional offices at locations determined by the Administrator. SBA announced a six-regional-office relocation policy in March 2025; this proposal adds statutory definitions, triggers, deadlines and noncompliance consequences rather than first creating all relocation authority or proving the announced moves occurred. Existing INA custody/officer authorities, read with enacted 119-1 custody amendments, remain qualified; the bill does not independently make every detainer lawful or compel every local officer to act. H.Res.458 supplies a deemed modified pending-bill substitute and later separate final-passage context; the exact EH text controls this passage, not the earlier committee version. Actual office closures/moves, staff transfers, head removal, local wrongdoing, detention/removal, service loss or enactment is not inferred.

The exact H.R.2966 EH proposal requires the SBA Administrator to ensure every application for a loan under Small Business Act 7(a) or Small Business Investment Act titleV includes individual-applicant/individual-owner dates of birth, specified citizenship/status and ownership certifications, a certification that no direct/indirect applicant-concern owner is an ineligible person, and alien-registration numbers for LPR individual applicants or owners. The positive certification is that an individual applicant is a U.S. citizen, U.S. national or LPR, or that an applicant concern or loan guarantor is 100 percent beneficially owned by individuals in those categories. The printed ineligible-person categories are an asylee, refugee, individual issued a visa to remain in the United States, nonimmigrant under any INA 101(a)(15) subparagraph, DACA deferred-action recipient, or alien present without lawful status under the defined immigration laws. Direct/indirect ownership, not merely controlling ownership, matters. Section 2(b) makes the applicant ineligible if a post-enactment submitted application lacks required information, or if the applicant concern has any direct/indirect ineligible owner, or the individual applicant is an ineligible person. The post-enactment submission condition is printed in the missing-information route; it is not an express universal grandfathering clause for the separate status routes or proof of cancellation of existing loans. Existing 7(a) and titleV loan authorities remain, including development-company financing; the bill does not create the loan programs or guarantee approval to every positively certified person. The effective June 1,2025 SBA SOP already limits 7(a)/504 financing to 100 percent qualifying direct/indirect owners and required guarantors, with citizenship/national/LPR status, residence/entity conditions, ineligible categories, verification and its own qualified divestment/limited-guaranty exceptions. The proposal supplies statutory requirements substantially overlapping those agency restrictions, not the first restriction on noncitizen-owned borrowing. It does not expressly reproduce every SOP lookback, residence, conditional-card or limited-guaranty provision; existing program requirements are not assumed repealed, nor are agency exceptions silently inserted into the bill's text. U.S. nationality and lawful permanent residence have distinct retained INA definitions. The bill's visa/asylee/refugee labels and positive LPR certification are preserved without adjudicating an individual's prior or adjusted status. No removal of immigration status, actual application denial, loan cancellation, benefit loss or enactment is established by this House passage choice. H.Res.458's pending substitute and separate passage boundary are retained; this is the whole exact EH bill, not a component vote.

The exact H.R.884 EH proposal prohibits any individual who is not a citizen of the United States from voting in an election for public office in the District of Columbia or in any D.C. ballot initiative or referendum. Its printed criterion is citizenship, not only unlawful presence or a particular visa/LPR category; noncitizen U.S. nationals are not converted into citizens by that terminology. The proposal also repeals the entire Local Resident Voting Rights Amendment Act of 2022, D.C.Law 24-242, and restores/revives each provision it amended or repealed as if that Act had not been enacted. The local Act created an exception to the qualified-elector citizenship requirement for local elections, not federal voting. Its definition of local election covers Mayor, Council chairman/members, Attorney General, State Board of Education and Advisory Neighborhood Commissioner, plus initiative, referendum, recall and charter-amendment measures. It also changed the no-other-voting-residence/right language from State/territory to State/territory/country, removed a citizenship-statement phrase from the specified registration lead-in, and replaced citizens with residents in the specified registration provision. Those statutory modifications are part of the repeal/restoration, not silently omitted as if the bill only changed one sentence. Other voter qualifications are not replaced with unrestricted eligibility for citizens, and the bill does not repeal the entire D.C.Election Code or every later election amendment. The local Act's effective/congressional-review provisions and budget-inclusion applicability condition are retained as baseline; the candidate makes no independent claim that a particular person was registered or voted under it. Existing 18 USC 611 already prohibits specified alien voting in federal-office elections, with the separately conducted authorized nonfederal-vote and parent/residence/reasonable-belief exceptions. H.R.884 extends a citizenship-based prohibition to the stated D.C. election/ballot scope and removes the local-law exception; it is not the first federal restriction on alien voting. It does not itself create naturalization, admission, removal or immigration-detention authority, prescribe a documentary-proof process, add a criminal penalty, or adjudicate the constitutional/enforcement consequences for an individual. H.Res.489 deems a pending committee substitute and provides a separate final-passage/recommit stage; this exact EH whole-bill passage has its own episode. Actual registration cancellation, ballot exclusion, crime, removal, loss of status, election effect or enactment is not inferred.

The exact H.R.2056 EH proposal prohibits the District of Columbia from having a statute, ordinance, policy or practice that prohibits or restricts a District government entity or official from sending, receiving, maintaining or exchanging information about any individual's citizenship or immigration status, lawful or unlawful, with any Federal, State or local government entity. It separately prohibits such District restrictions on compliance with a lawfully made DHS request under INA 236 or 287 to comply with a detainer for, or notify about release of, an individual. This is an express D.C.-specific restriction on governmental policies/practices. Existing 8 USC 1373 and 1644 already contain statutory restrictions on limiting certain status-information exchanges with the immigration service; the bill is not the first general permission to communicate immigration status. The bill's printed information clause includes citizenship as well as status and communication with any listed governmental entity, while its separate lawful-request clause specifically addresses detainers/release notices. INA 236 and 287 already govern qualified immigration custody and officer powers, including specified custody/release conditions, arrest limits and cooperation provisions. H.R.2056 does not itself rewrite those authorities, deem every DHS request lawful, or establish that every individual detainer must be obeyed. It bars District policies restricting the specified lawful-request compliance; individual custody legality, actual information disclosure/detention/removal, implementation and enactment are not inferred.

The complete H.R.1998 EH creates a conditional sanctions scheme separate from its findings and nonbinding global anti-piracy statements. The President must impose the described sanctions for a foreign person determined knowingly to engage in piracy. Foreign person excludes the printed U.S.-person categories: U.S. citizens, permanent resident aliens and U.S.-organized entities including foreign branches; unlike H.R.36 this definition does not exclude every person merely located in the United States. Section4(b)(1) property blocking is MAY despite the general SHALL in4(a), and dispenses with1701 emergency prerequisites. The immigration route applies to an INA alien whom State or DHS, or either designee, knows or has reason to believe is described in4(a): inadmissibility, no visa/entry documentation, no admission/parole or any other INA benefit. The issuing consular officer, State, DHS or a designee SHALL revoke the qualifying alien visa/entry documentation in accordance with existing INA221(i), regardless of issuance date, with immediate effect cancelling other valid entry documents. Existing221(i) already gives consular officers/State discretionary anytime revocation, notice to the Attorney General, invalidation from issuance, protected carrier reliance absent due notice, and the qualified judicial-review limitation/sole-ground removal-proceeding exception. The new targeted mandatory rule and listed DHS actor are not the first visa-revocation authority; the candidate does not infer repeal of the incorporated safeguards. Piracy expressly means ANY act violating ANY provision of18 USCchapter81, not only a violent seizure at sea. The chapter includes law-of-nations/high-seas piracy, citizenship/treaty-qualified foreign commissions or war, privateer arming/service, violent obstruction of a commander, vessel/property conversion or surrender, corrupt assistance/trading/confederacy, distress-vessel plunder, escape obstruction/false lights, malicious vessel attack, knowing receipt of pirate property and robbery ashore from a piratical cruise, each with its own elements/jurisdiction. These are existing predicates, not new criminal offenses or a claim that every offense can apply to every foreign person; the bill determination/knowledge test does not expressly require conviction. Necessary admission OR parole for UN-headquarters/other international obligations is excepted, with the printed reference to sanctions with respect to admission retained. Qualified agricultural/food/medicine/device, humanitarian, finance and necessary transport transactions are excepted, as are authorized U.S. intelligence, law-enforcement and national-security activities. No importation-of-goods sanctions authority is added and no family extension is stated. The President may waive sanctions after certifying to House Foreign Affairs and Senate Foreign Relations at least 15 days before effectiveness that the waiver is CRUCIAL to U.S. national-security interests; this bill states no 180-day maximum. Existing IEEPA implementation and penalties apply to specified regulatory violations, preserving criminal willfulness/conviction rather than equating sanctions designation with a criminal judgment. Classified evidence may be submitted ex parte/in camera in an existing judicial review, without creating a review right. The recorded suspension-and-passage as amended concerns the entire EH, a separate bill episode; no actual piracy, designation, visa cancellation, removal, enforcement outcome or enactment is inferred.

The exact H.R.875 EH proposal adds INA 212(a)(2)(J) inadmissibility for any alien convicted of, admitting commission of, or admitting acts constituting the essential elements of an intoxicated/impaired-driving offense. The terms take their meaning under the law of the jurisdiction where the conviction, offense or essential acts occurred, expressly including alcohol/drug influence or impairment, without regard to misdemeanor/felony classification under Federal, State, tribal or local law. Existing INA 212(a) makes inadmissibility relevant to visas and admission. It separately adds INA 237(a)(2)(G) deportability for conviction of a jurisdiction-defined intoxicated/impaired-driving offense, including alcohol/drug influence or impairment, regardless of the listed misdemeanor/felony classification. That clause uses the law where conviction occurred and does not make admission of conduct alone its predicate. Neither clause requires an injury/death or multiple offenses. The existing INA 101(a)(48) conviction framework remains, including specified withheld-adjudication situations with guilt/plea/facts and court-ordered punishment/penalty/restraint. These are additional categorical statutory grounds, rather than a claim that covered conduct previously could never trigger other criminal inadmissibility or deportability. Existing criminal INA grounds retain their own elements and exceptions. The single-offense minor/petty-offense exception in 212(a)(2)(A), the enumerated 212(h) waiver, and the 237(a)(2)(A)(vi) pardon exception are not printed exceptions to new J/G. Existing discretionary temporary-nonimmigrant/T/U inadmissibility waiver routes are retained within their own conditions; no categorical relief, guilt or automatic deportation is inferred. The bill concerns any alien meeting the grounds, not only a person unlawfully present. The new 237(a)(2) deportability ground sits within the existing 237(a) framework for an alien (including a crewman) in and admitted to the United States, with removal upon the specified government order. The complete January 12 H.R. 2683 EH suspension-and-passage proposal adds remote access to the Export Control Reform Act framework. New section 1742(15) defines remote access as access on a purposeful, knowing, reckless OR negligent basis to an item subject to U.S. jurisdiction under the Act BY A FOREIGN PERSON through a network connection, including internet/cloud services, FROM A LOCATION OTHER THAN THE ITEM'S PHYSICAL LOCATION, IF Commerce determines that use of the item could pose a SERIOUS national-security or foreign-policy risk. Neither overseas location, China connection nor a particular AI model is printed as a universal trigger. Items include commodities, software and technology; the item/risk/jurisdiction/network/different-location/foreign-person conditions matter. Ordinary internet use or every cloud service is not automatically prohibited, and the bill does not supply a specific new list of controlled models, devices, countries or individual licenses.
The material Immigration boundary is the direct natural-person eligibility predicate, not national-security rhetoric or predicted immigration consequences. Existing 4801(5)(A) expressly excludes from foreign person a U.S. citizen, a LAWFUL PERMANENT RESIDENT, or another protected individual under8 U.S.C. 1324b(a)(3). The imported definition covers citizens OR nationals and specified LPR, lawful temporary residence under 1160(a)/1255a(a)(1), refugee and asylum statuses, with its naturalization application/pursuit/time qualifications. LPR exclusion is also an INDEPENDENT explicit route in4801(5)(A); a qualification on the imported protected-individual route does not erase that separate LPR exclusion. Not all foreign-born people, noncitizens, visa holders or persons physically in the United States have the same covered status. Immigration/nationality status directly affects whether a natural person is the foreign recipient of the newly regulated access; it does not grant or alter that immigration status, naturalization, visas, work authorization or INA admission/removal. Importing the definition does not import all employment-discrimination remedies, exemptions or a right to employment. The entity branch separately includes defined non-U.S.-incorporated/organized businesses and other entities, international organizations, foreign governments/agencies; that branch is not an immigration-status determination about every employee, owner or national. Existing 4801(13)U.S. person includes, for subchapterI, qualified nationals/protected individuals, organized legal entities AND any person IN THE UNITED STATES; U.S. person and foreign person are not simple complements. Providers and other U.S. persons can have duties even when they are not foreign-person recipients. No unrestricted-access entitlement for every citizen/LPR or blanket criminal exemption is established.
The proposal adds risk-qualified foreign-person remote access to the President's SHALL-control authority and the corresponding SHALL-regulate duty in4812, carried out through established policy objectives and the framework for regulations, controlled-item/person/end-use lists and guidance. It extends Commerce's existing 4813 prohibitions on UNAUTHORIZED transfers, restrictions for listed foreign persons/end uses, licensing/conditions/suspension/revocation, foreign-availability assessment, compliance/information, inspection/seizure/temporary denial, monitoring, license-required notice and enhanced controls to the specified remote-access settings. This is regulatory authority and specified duties, not an immediate statutory ban on every covered access, mandatory denial of every foreign person's application or a free license for excluded natural persons. Separate extended enhanced controls apply to U.S. persons and the named weapons/nuclear-project activities, with retained material-contribution denial standard and other-agency authorization exception. Existing 4813(b) retains the IEEPA 1702(b)limits on items that cannot be regulated, including qualified personal communications, humanitarian articles, information/materials and travel transactions, with the printed donation determinations/information-control exceptions. No universal exemption for every data/model/software transaction or repeal of other sanctions/export authorities is inferred. Existing terrorism-country licensing has its country/item/State determinations and30-day congressional notice; it is not a new immigration visa ground or a citizenship-wide country ban.
H.R. 2683 extends the existing interagency person-list/end-use monitoring criteria, Commerce licensing/authorization procedure, prospective compliance assistance, penalties, enforcement/confidentiality and interagency control-coordination clauses. Retained expeditious/transparent licensing and no-application-fee framework matters; the thirty-day processing wording is a SENSE OF CONGRESS best-efforts standard, not automatic approval or a newly imposed hard thirty-day deadline. Existing compliance assistance/security-clearance provisions are not new immigration-clearance or visa powers. The new congressional-consultation section requires Commerce to keep House Foreign Affairs and Senate Banking committees fully/currently informed of anticipated remote-access regulations, including risk, method and economic effect, in classified settings as necessary. It expressly does NOT require their approval as a condition of exercising ECRA authority. No public disclosure of classified information or committee veto is created.
The definition's purposeful/knowing/reckless/negligent range expressly does NOT lower criminal mens rea under section 1760. Existing 4819(b) WILLFUL criminal violation/attempt/conspiracy or aiding/abetting framework, statutory maximum fine of $1 million and individual imprisonment up to 20 years, including the printed AND and OR BOTH clause, is retained rather than new strict-liability imprisonment for negligent access. Those are statutory maxima, not a current inflation-adjusted civil-dollar quote or an individual sentence. Civil authority can include fine, license revocation and extended ability-to-access/provide-access prohibition, with notice/opportunity for agency hearing. The specified false-document/report and remote-access provisions are within the retained unlawful-act framework. Existing prior-CONVICTION authority is DISCRETIONARY: it may deny remote-access/provision eligibility for ANY item, WHETHER OR NOT controlled, for up to 10 years or revoke interested licenses for the listed offenses; related-party extension requires a shown affiliation/ownership/control/responsibility/trade connection and retained hearing procedures. It is not automatic guilt or immigration removal of family members. Existing criminal/civil forfeiture and other administrative/judicial/settlement powers remain context, not a new INA consequence. Enforcement search/detain/seize/temporary-denial authorities concern covered items/conveyances and suspected control violations; they do not create new immigration detention/removal authority because DHS can participate. Confidential licensing/reporting/enforcement information retains specified withholding/national-interest, Congress/GAO and qualified interagency sharing rules.

The exact H.J.Res.72 EH proposition terminates the national emergency identified by the President's February 1, 2025 finding in Executive Order 14193, using National Emergencies Act section 202. Under 50 USC 1622(a), powers or authorities exercised by reason of that identified emergency cease after termination, subject to savings for prior actions and unfinished proceedings, actions based on earlier acts, and matured rights/duties or incurred penalties. EO 14193 section 1 both expands the scope of the earlier southern-border emergency and declares/reiterates an NEA/IEEPA emergency concerning Canada. Its operative package imposes Canadian-product tariffs and related customs/foreign-trade-zone measures, assigns implementation/reporting duties, and in section 3(b) requires the DHS Secretary, coordinating with the specified officials, to recommend additional action if Canada fails to take adequate steps to alleviate illegal migration and illicit-drug crises through cooperative enforcement actions. That immigration-specific governmental recommendation duty is operative text, not merely a preamble prediction. Independent Immigration membership rests on terminating the identified emergency authority and its direct immigration-cooperation governance, without importing every mechanism from the earlier southern-border proclamation. This does not resolve every legal consequence of their overlapping emergency scopes. The candidate does not claim that the resolution independently repeals every January 20 military, detention, barrier or INA authority, orders Canada to cooperate, removes all tariffs under other authority, or changes an individual's immigration status. The underlying general NEA termination/savings framework and IEEPA authorities are retained; the proposed change is termination of this identified emergency rather than a new immigration power. The House choice concerns the complete emergency-termination proposition, including its trade and other purposes, rather than a separate vote on a particular tariff, recommendation or immigration program. Actual termination, executive action, tariff effects, cooperation, admission, detention, removal or enactment is not established by the House vote.

The February 11 House passage of S. 1383 adopts the complete SAVE America replacement in EAH, not the veterans-advisory body named in the retained Clerk title. Section 2 replaces NVRA section 4(b)'s existing continuously-qualified no-registration/same-day-registration State exemptions with documentary citizenship requirements for any registration method and adds a special confirmation system for a State/jurisdiction that does not require registration. NVRA State means the fifty States and DC; Federal-office scope is not every local election. Documentary proof has five alternative routes: citizenship-indicating REAL ID identification; valid U.S. passport; official military ID TOGETHER WITH military service record showing U.S. birth; valid Federal/State/Tribal photo ID showing U.S. birth; or other such photo ID TOGETHER WITH specified certified birth record, contemporaneous hospital extract, final adoption decree, Consular Report/certification of citizen birth abroad, naturalization/citizenship or other Federal INA proof, or DHS KIC card. The certified birth-record route has all listed issuer/file/name/date/place/parent/signature/seal requirements. Military ID alone is not the citizenship-proof route. REAL ID law permits many noncitizen statuses: the bill's first route additionally requires an indication of citizenship, not any compliant ID. Existing 22 U.S.C. 212 permits passports for noncitizen nationals; the literal valid-passport route is preserved alongside the citizenship requirement, without deciding individual eligibility or equating national with citizen. INA alien excludes both citizens and nationals; noncitizen and alien are not interchangeable.
The proposal requires acceptance/processing for a name discrepancy when otherwise qualifying proof is accompanied by required name-change documentation OR the State-process affidavit of prior name. Applicants without the listed documentary proof have a State process: sworn citizen/eligible attestation, OTHER EVIDENCE, official sufficiency determination and an official uniform EAC affidavit explaining the basis. Other discrepancies have an additional-documentation process. Attestation alone is not automatic registration. Motor-vehicle/agencies/mail forms and verification are amended; mail registration requires in-person proof at the election office by the State deadline or at a qualifying same-day polling place by election day, with notice/instructions and reasonable disability accommodations. New absent-uniformed-services applicants under 20310(1) are excepted from section 2 requirements; that defined category includes qualified service/merchant-marine members and their spouses/dependents absent from residence by reason of service, not every civilian overseas citizen. The State exemption savings concerns OTHER Federal laws, not retention of the replaced NVRA exemption. Registration amendments take effect at enactment for applications submitted on/after enactment.
Within 30 days States must establish ongoing citizenship-checking programs, submit their COMPLETE official Federal voter list to DHS for SAVE comparison and take removal steps after NOTICE and OPPORTUNITYto provide citizenship proof; a preexisting purpose-qualified DHSagreement may satisfy this duty. Other State data are optional, and Social Security-agreement information cannot be the SOLEground for removing a voter. Existing 405(r)(9) matches name/date/SSN/deceased records and has confidentiality/exception restrictions; no infallible citizenship database or individual noncitizenship is established. Federal departments possessing relevant eligibility information must provide necessary verification information, including requested batches, within 24 hours of a State request, share information and not charge the State a response fee. Printed SAVEresponse paragraph(1) reference and information-sharing paragraph(A) reference remain literal, not silently repaired. DHS SHALL investigate WHETHER to initiatesection 239 removal proceedings if an ALIEN is determined pursuant to the specified information provisions to be unlawfully registered for Federal elections. This is not automatic removal, conviction, investigation of every noncitizen list match or a new universal deportation ground. Existing section 239 notice/counsel/proceeding distinctions remain; existing 121(c)(1) noncriminal-enforcement-use bar creates an explicit review dependency, not an assumed repeal.
Section 2 adds noncitizen documentation/verified-information roll-removal grounds and at-any-time language, with the specified 90-day-systematic-removal exception amendment. List deletion is distinct from immigration removal. Mail form document-recording and qualified criminal/immigration evidentiary confidentiality exceptions are printed separately: motor-vehicle exception uses KNOWING attempts/false declarations, while mail exception omits those express words. Private civil enforcement adds missing-proof registration to covered violations but retains notice/cure and existing remedies. The amended 20511(2) criminal mechanism retains KNOWING AND WILLFUL fair-election deprivation/fraud/attempt elements; new executive-branch material assistance and missing-proof registration categories do not create strict-liability imprisonment for every mistaken official. Existing penalty is fine and/or up to five years. EAC registration guidance is due 10 days after enactment; voter-material development/modification is exempted from PRA; DHS must promptly notify the domicile State chief election official upon receiving naturalization information. Section 2 preserves provisional casting and counting if citizenship is verified under the new process, without waiving separate photo-ID ballot rules. Existing Federal alien-voting prohibition under section 611 and its mixed-election/qualified-belief exceptions are baseline, not newly created or repealed.
Section 3 adds HAVA section 303A photo-identification requirements for Federal ballots, not citizenship conferred by possessing photo ID. An in-person voter needs valid PHYSICAL photo ID; lacking it permits a provisional ballot but eligibility determination requires within THREE DAYS either the required ID or the State affidavit of religious objection to being photographed. Other reasons for provisional voting remain governed by their existing rules. The complete H.R. 2189 EH adds a narrowly defined less-than-lethal projectile-device exception to the second sentence of 18 USC 921(a)(3), alongside its pre-existing antique-firearm exception, and adds paragraph (39). This is not solely a label for general criminal enforcement: existing INA 237(a)(2)(C) expressly incorporates FIREARM OR DESTRUCTIVE DEVICE as defined in 921(a), and existing 922(g)(5) regulates firearms/ammunition using illegal or unlawful presence or admission under a nonimmigrant visa. The candidate domain connection is those express definition/status links, not presumed immigration consequences from a crime. The firearm branch of the incorporated definition would acquire the new exception. The separate 921(a)(4) destructive-device definition is NOT amended by TitleI, and the INA ground separately includes destructive devices; a qualifying-device label therefore does not establish exemption from every branch or every other immigration ground. Existing 237(a)applies to an alien IN AND ADMITTED TO the United States, with removal upon the specified order, and 237(a)(2)(C)requires an after-admission CONVICTION under any law of the specified purchase/sale/exchange/use/ownership/possession/carrying or attempt/conspiracy conduct involving a qualifying weapon, part or accessory in violation of law. Arrest, allegation or a conduct admission alone is not this conviction predicate. No individual device classification, state-conviction comparison, adjudication, cancellation of an existing order or actual avoidance of removal is inferred. The new device must satisfy ALL printed criteria: not designed/intended to expel, nor readily convertible to accept/discharge, common handgun/rifle/shotgun ammunition or any other projectile above 500 feet/second; designed/intended use not likely to cause death or serious bodily injury; and unable to accept or be readily modified to accept a feeding device loaded through a pistol grip or commonly used in semiautomatic firearms. It is not every less-lethal weapon, every projectile device or a universal harmlessness finding. The AG must make a requested device determination within 90 days AFTER RECEIVING THE DEVICE; the deadline is not automatic approval or compulsory classification of every product. Existing 922(g)(5) and (y) status predicates, hunting/sport/license, foreign-official and friendly-government law-enforcement exceptions and qualified AG waiver remain baseline; not all noncitizens are prohibited. Existing ammunition is separately defined by 921(a)(17), so the proposal is not a blanket permission to possess otherwise regulated ammunition or ordinary firearms. It confers no nationality, visa, lawful presence, admission, work authorization or unrestricted weapons right. TitleII separately adds 4181 excise-tax exemptions for the defined devices, devices on the Secretary annual list meeting the criteria except the above 500 velocity criterion, and specified shells/cartridges with the printed design/use conditions; adds 90 day classification duties, annual lists/reports, and expands the distinct 5845(a)NFA definition exclusions to those device categories. The TAX listed-above 500 category is not inserted into TitleI 921(a)(39) and cannot be imported into the INA firearm-definition exception. Section 202 sales apply after enactment; qualifying requests in the first 180 days are treated as received at the close of that period for the 90 day rule. No special retroactive immigration/conviction rule is printed. Existing 4182 military, small-manufacturer and paid-NFA exemptions, existing 5845 antique/qualified collector-device exclusions, and enacted 119-21 section 70436 zero transfer/making-tax and 4182(a)conforming provisions are retained context, so this is not the first federal device exemption or tax relief and not a claim every affected product previously paid the same tax. These are distinct criminal, immigration-incorporation and tax objects. The exact whole-bill final-passage choice includes BOTH titles, not a separate vote on the removal ground, noncitizen possession or an individual device. One H.R. 2189 episode; the failed 1042 and adopted 1057 rules only established proposed/pending consideration and do not add independent policy findings. No actual sales, tax savings, public-safety effect or enactment is inferred.

The exact H.R.1958 EH proposal adds INA 212(a)(2)(J) inadmissibility and 237(a)(2)(G) deportability for an alien convicted of, admitting commission of, or admitting acts constituting the essential elements of any listed offense. Both clauses allow specified admissions, despite the title's conviction-only wording. The list is: SNAP offenses under 7 USC 2024; Social Security Act 208/42 USC 408 offenses;18 USC 666 theft/bribery concerning federally funded programs;1028 identification-document/authentication/identity offenses;1031 major federal fraud; any offense under title 18chapter 63;371 federal-offense/government-fraud conspiracy; any other offense involving defrauding the United States Government or unlawful receipt of a defined Federal/State/local public benefit; and conspiracy to commit any of those. These incorporate criminal offenses with their own elements, not every administrative overpayment, eligibility mistake, suspicion or civil injunction. The enumerated statutes are not narrowed by the bill's government-fraud title: chapter 63 includes mail/wire/bank fraud, health-care fraud, securities/commodities fraud, qualifying false corporate financial certification, foreign labor-contracting fraud, foreign-official bribery and attempts/conspiracies. Its civil injunction and definition provisions are not themselves new criminal offenses. A healthcare-benefit program under 18 USC 24 can be public or private and must affect commerce. The predicate statutes retain material qualifications. SNAP knowing unauthorized-use/presentation crimes include low-value misdemeanors, with value-based penalty tiers; the bill adds no felony-only or universal loss threshold. Section 666 requires the stated$5,000 property/transaction threshold and an entity receiving more than$10,000 federal-program benefits in the specified year, and excludes ordinary-course bona fide compensation/expenses. Section 1031 requires knowing execution/attempt with the specified fraud intent in federal assistance/procurement valued at least$1 million, not necessarily$1 million loss. Section 1028 retains its identified knowing/intent predicates, document/commerce/mail/federal nexus (including the five-or-more document/feature condition for 1028(a)(3)) and authorized investigative/protective/intelligence exceptions. Section 371 requires at least two conspirators and an act to effect the object. Section 408 retains its distinct false-statement/conversion/identity/number/disclosure offenses and narrow legacy-adjustment prosecution exception, with its specified carveouts; that prosecution exception is not represented as blanket immunity from the new INA clauses. The benefit catchall uses 1611(c)/1621(c) definitions encompassing specified grants/contracts/loans/licenses and household/individual retirement, welfare, health, disability, housing, education, food, unemployment or similar assistance. Their employment-related nonimmigrant/compact, treaty-benefit and foreign-professional-license exceptions remain; State/local benefit also excludes Federal benefit under 1611(c). The catchall requires an offense involving unlawful receipt, not merely receipt by a noncitizen, and does not itself repeal those definitions' exclusions. Section 2(c) makes a person described in the newJ orG ineligible for any relief under the immigration laws, expressly including PublicLaw 105-277 section 2242. That incorporated statute implements the policy against involuntary return where substantial grounds indicate danger of torture, with its stated treaty/reservation, exclusion and review conditions. The bill expressly seeks a broad relief bar rather than merely new admission grounds; no actual return to torture, individual adjudication or conclusion about treaty/constitutional enforceability is inferred. INA 101's immigration-laws definition includes relevant laws, conventions and treaties. The relief clause expressly identifies INA 212(a)(2)(J) but prints 8 USC 1128 in its parenthetical; that citation irregularity is preserved and disclosed, not silently repaired. The offenses and existing criminal INA grounds predate this proposal; the new clauses add immigration grounds and a separate relief bar. Existing moral-turpitude/aggravated-felony conditions are not treated as thresholds for these new clauses, and their narrow waivers/exceptions are not represented as overriding the new relief bar. Whole-bill passage does not establish guilt, actual denial/deportation, a component preference or enactment. The new 237(a)(2) deportability ground sits within the existing 237(a) framework for an alien (including a crewman) in and admitted to the United States, with removal upon the specified government order. It is not a universal new deportability ground for every unadmitted alien. INA 101 distinguishes immigration admission (lawful entry after inspection/authorization) from admitting criminal conduct; parole alone is not admission. This governing status scope is separate from any offense's after-admission timing element. No individual admission status or actual removal order is inferred.

The complete H.R. 5103 EH establishes a statutory District of Columbia Safe and Beautiful Commission in the executive branch.
